claim: Reinforcement learning, driven by success and failure, is fundamental to sensorimotor learning.
source: Reinforcement learning, driven by success and failure, is fundamental to such sensorimotor learning.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of reinforcement learning in sensorimotor learning, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The study engaged children aged 3–17 years and adults in a cross-sectional sample of N=385 using online motor tasks.
source: We studied the development of reinforcement motor learning using online motor tasks to engage children aged 3–17 years and adults (cross-sectional sample, N=385).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample size, age range, and study design.

claim: Learning was incomplete or absent in 3–8 year-olds in the continuous probabilistic task.
source: Learning was incomplete or absent in 3–8 year-olds and gradually improved to adult-like levels by adolescence.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings regarding learning performance in young children.

claim: Learning gradually improved to adult-like levels by adolescence.
source: Learning was incomplete or absent in 3–8 year-olds and gradually improved to adult-like levels by adolescence.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the developmental trajectory observed in the study.

claim: A reinforcement learning model identified two age-dependent factors underlying improvement: increasing exploration after failed movements and decreasing motor noise.
source: A reinforcement learning model fit to each participant identified two age-dependent factors underlying improvement across development: an increasing amount of exploration after a failed movement and a decreasing level of motor noise.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's findings regarding developmental factors.

claim: Switching to discrete targets and deterministic reward improved 3–8 year-olds' learning to adult-like levels by increasing exploration after failed movements.
source: We predicted, and confirmed, that switching to discrete targets and deterministic reward would improve 3–8 year-olds' learning to adult-like levels by increasing exploration after failed movements.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a prediction that was confirmed by experimental data.

claim: A 9-week-old infant will increase kicking frequency when a ribbon connects their foot to an overhead mobile that moves with their kicks.
source: For example, a 9-week-old infant will increase kicking frequency when a ribbon connects their foot to an overhead mobile that moves with their kicks (Rovee and Rovee, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Three-month-olds can learn to produce a specific kick height to move a mobile.
source: Three-month-olds can even learn to produce a specific kick height to move a mobile (Sargent et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Children aged 3 to 9 years old showed different sensitivities to reward probability in a probabilistic reaching task.
source: In a more complex probabilistic reaching task, children aged 3 to 9 years old showed different sensitivities to reward probability (Stevenson and Weir, 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Younger children (3-9 years) were more likely to stick on a rewarded target even if the reward rate was low (e.g. 33%).
source: The youngest aged children were more likely to stick on a rewarded target even if the reward rate was low (e.g. 33%), whereas older children explored other targets.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study (Stevenson and Weir, 1959).

claim: Younger children are less likely to explore new options and are more willing to accept lower reward rates.
source: This suggests that younger children are less likely to explore new options and are more willing to accept lower reward rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about children's behavior in reward tasks.

claim: 2-year-old children could accurately select a reinforced visual image from two choices.
source: In a relatively simple task, 2-year-old children could accurately select a reinforced visual image from two choices (de Sousa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Children (7–12 years old) were unable to use information about hidden factors to optimize their choices in a probabilistic reward environment.
source: Although children (7–12 years old) and adolescents (13–17 years old) could identify the factors in the environment that changed the outcome, children were unable to use this information to optimize their choices.
evidence: This is a description of findings from previous research on cognitive reinforcement learning tasks.

claim: Probabilistic reasoning improves with age from 8 to 25 years old.
source: Similarly, Schulz et al., 2016 used a sequential learning task (8–25 year olds) to show that probabilistic reasoning improves with age.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Schulz et al., 2016).

claim: Sensorimotor tasks involve different combinations of motor and cognitive mechanisms.
source: Sensorimotor tasks involve different combinations of motor and cognitive mechanisms (Chen et al., 2017; McDougle et al., 2016), and there are both implicit and explicit (cognitive) contributions to reinforcement motor learning (Holland et al., 2018; van Mastrigt et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There are both implicit and explicit (cognitive) contributions to reinforcement motor learning.
source: Sensorimotor tasks involve different combinations of motor and cognitive mechanisms (Chen et al., 2017; McDougle et al., 2016), and there are both implicit and explicit (cognitive) contributions to reinforcement motor learning (Holland et al., 2018; van Mastrigt et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Holland et al., 2018; van Mastrigt et al., 2023).

claim: The study included 298 children aged 3–17 years and 87 adults from across the USA.
source: We developed a remote video game paradigm for a cross-sectional study of 298 children aged 3–17 years and 87 adults from across the USA (locations and demographics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample composition and references tables and figures showing demographics.

claim: Exploration variability increases with age in children.
source: We hypothesized that children's reinforcement learning abilities would improve with age and depend on the developmental trajectory of exploration variability, learning rate (how much people adjust their reach after success), and motor noise (here defined as all sources of noise associated with movement, including sensory noise, memory noise, and motor noise).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis that was tested in the study, and the results confirmed this developmental trajectory.

claim: Motor noise decreases with age in children.
source: Using a mechanistic model, we show that this improvement is due to a developmental gradient of increasing exploration after failure and reducing motor noise with age.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings from the mechanistic model.

claim: Use of deterministic feedback and discrete targets can dramatically improve learning abilities of younger children.
source: Importantly, we then show that use of deterministic feedback and discrete targets can dramatically improve learning abilities of younger children.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings from experimental manipulation.

claim: All participants but one performed well in the baseline block of the task.
source: All participants but one performed well in the baseline block of the task, with endpoint position on average within the target zone (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about baseline performance with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: Participants could accurately hit discrete targets in the baseline block.
source: This shows that participants could accurately hit discrete targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the baseline performance data showing endpoints within target zones.

claim: The 5- and 7-year-old children showed exploration but little sensitivity to previous failure versus success.
source: Figure 2b shows the 5- and 7-year-old children moved to many endpoint locations (i.e. showed exploration) receiving reward based on the probability landscape. Interestingly, their exploration appeared to show little sensitivity to previous failure (open circles) versus success (filled circles) and endpoints did not converge on the 100% reward zone (gray area) by the end of the block.
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior patterns in Figure 2b for specific age groups.

claim: Older children (aged 11, 12, and 15) performed similarly to adults, exploring early and then focusing movements on the 100% reward zone.
source: The older children, aged 11, 12, and 15, performed similarly to the adult, exploring early in the block, and then focusing movements on the unseen 100% reward zone.
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior patterns for older children compared to adults.

claim: On average, the 3–5 and 6–8 year-olds did not find the 100% reward zone.
source: These patterns were also observed in group data (Figure 3, binned across 6 age groups) where, on average, the 3–5 and 6–8 year-olds did not find the 100% reward zone, but the older age groups did.
evidence: This is a direct statement about group-level performance with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Accuracy of movement to discrete targets was maintained throughout the experiment even for younger children.
source: For participants aged 3–17 years, an ANOVA of accuracy (distance from discrete target center) by block (first vs. last) and age (5 bins) shows no effect of block (F1,106=0.282, p=0.597) and no interaction between age and block (F4,106=1.219, p=0.307), indicating that accuracy of movement to discrete targets was maintained throughout the experiment even for the younger children.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results showing no change in accuracy across blocks.

claim: In younger children, movements tended to be more curved compared to older children, as indicated by larger path length ratios.
source: In younger children, movements tended to be more curved compared to older children, as indicated by larger path length ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about movement characteristics with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Movement times were similar for all children.
source: Movement times were similar for all children (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), but younger children took longer to initiate a trial by clicking on the ball (longer Reaction Time) and start moving after initiating (longer Stationary Time).
evidence: This is a direct statement about timing parameters with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Younger children took longer to initiate a trial (longer Reaction Time) and start moving after initiating (longer Stationary Time).
source: Movement times were similar for all children (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), but younger children took longer to initiate a trial by clicking on the ball (longer Reaction Time) and start moving after initiating (longer Stationary Time).
evidence: This is a direct statement about timing differences with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Baseline precision (endpoint variability relative to target center) decreased significantly with age.
source: In the Baseline block, the endpoint variability relative to target center (Baseline precision) decreased significantly with age (Figure 4a; regression R2 = 0.153, F1,109 = 19.7, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: Baseline precision findings are consistent with known developmental changes in motor variability.
source: This is consistent with known developmental changes in motor variability (Takahashi et al., 2003; Deutsch and Newell, 2005) and may represent one component of motor noise that is distinct from exploration.
evidence: This claim connects the study's findings to previous research through citations.

claim: Distance from the target (averaged over the last 10 reaches) significantly reduced with age.
source: The distance from the target, averaged over the last 10 reaches, significantly reduced with age (Figure 4b; regression R2 = 0.256, F1,109 = 37.4, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Younger children rarely reached the 100% reward zone, whereas children over 9 years old often did.
source: Younger children rarely reached the 100% reward zone (gray region), whereas children over 9 years old often did.
evidence: This is a direct statement about age-related differences in reaching the reward zone.

claim: Adults showed high variability after failure and low variability after success.
source: Adults showed high variability after failure and low variability after success, as expected.
evidence: This is a direct statement about adult behavior in the clamp conditions.

claim: Variability after failure was low in younger children and increased significantly with age.
source: In children, variability after failure was low in younger children and increased significantly with age (regression R2 = 0.17, F1,109 = 22.3, p<0.001), doubling across the age range to reach adult levels (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Variability after success was relatively stable across age.
source: In contrast, variability after success was relatively stable across age (regression R2 = 0.012, F1,109 = 1.34, p=0.249).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results showing no significant age effect.

claim: Younger children do not explore as much as older children after failures.
source: Overall, these results suggest that younger children do not explore as much as older children after failures, which is essential to finding the reward zone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability data in the clamp conditions.

claim: Model 11 was the preferred model with a ΔBIC = 216 to the next best model.
source: Model 11 was the preferred model with a ΔBIC = 216 to the next best model (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of model selection results with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The same model (Model 11) was preferred when only using BICs from each of the two tasks separately for either the children alone or including the adults.
source: The same model was preferred when we only used BICs from each of the two tasks separately for either the children alone or including the adults.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the robustness of model selection across different subsets of data.

claim: The value-based model was not preferred to Model 11 (ΔBIC = 3018) when fitting the children in the Continuous probabilistic task.
source: This model was not preferred to Model 11 (ΔBIC = 3018) when fitting the children in the Continuous probabilistic task.
evidence: This is a direct statement of model comparison results.

claim: In the preferred model, if the previous trial was a failure, the current reach is the desired reach with the addition of exploration variability and motor noise.
source: In this model, if the previous trial was a failure (Figure 5a, top), the current reach is the desired reach with the addition of exploration variability and motor noise.
evidence: This is a direct description of the preferred model's mechanics with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: The desired reach is updated only if the current reach is successful.
source: The desired reach for the next trial is updated only if the current reach is successful.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model's update rule.

claim: If the previous reach was a success, the participant does not explore so that the current reach is the desired reach with motor noise.
source: In contrast, if the previous reach was a success (Figure 5a, bottom), the participant does not explore so that the current reach is the desired reach with motor noise.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model's behavior after success with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Motor noise decreased by about 40% within the age range tested.
source: Motor noise decreased by about 40% within the age range tested.
evidence: This is a direct statement quantifying the developmental change in motor noise.

claim: Exploration variability increased with age, with an almost fourfold increase on average from the youngest to the oldest child.
source: Exploration variability increased with age, with an almost fourfold increase on average from the youngest to the oldest child.
evidence: This is a direct statement quantifying the developmental change in exploration variability.

claim: The increased motor noise and reduced exploration limit the ability of the younger children to learn efficiently.
source: Overall, this model analysis suggests that the increased motor noise and reduced exploration limit the ability of the younger children to learn efficiently.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model parameter estimates and their developmental trajectories.

claim: The model simulations with fit parameters accounted for the differences in learning across the age group bins.
source: The simulations of the model with the fit parameters accounted for the differences in learning across the age group bins (Figure 3 red line and shading show model simulations).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model fit quality with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The model could explain 16% and 42% of the variance for the success and fail clamp phases.
source: We also examined the model fits against the empirical data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4c and d), which showed we could explain 16% and 42% of the variance for the success and fail clamp phases (note that we only have 9 trials to calculate each clamp block standard deviation).
evidence: This is a direct statement of variance explained with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Discretizing the target appeared to improve the learning for the two youngest age groups.
source: Discretizing the target appeared to improve the learning for the two youngest age groups (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of discrete targets with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, distance from target decreased with age (R2=0.074, F1,104 = 8.31, p=0.0048).
source: That is, distance from target decreased with age (R2=0.074, F1,104 = 8.31, p=0.0048), baseline precision improved with age (R2=0.150, F1,104 = 18.4, p<0.001) and fail clamp variability increased with age (R2=0.162, F1,104 = 20.1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the discrete probabilistic task.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, baseline precision improved with age (R2=0.150, F1,104 = 18.4, p<0.001).
source: That is, distance from target decreased with age (R2=0.074, F1,104 = 8.31, p=0.0048), baseline precision improved with age (R2=0.150, F1,104 = 18.4, p<0.001) and fail clamp variability increased with age (R2=0.162, F1,104 = 20.1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the discrete probabilistic task.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, fail clamp variability increased with age (R2=0.162, F1,104 = 20.1, p<0.001).
source: That is, distance from target decreased with age (R2=0.074, F1,104 = 8.31, p=0.0048), baseline precision improved with age (R2=0.150, F1,104 = 18.4, p<0.001) and fail clamp variability increased with age (R2=0.162, F1,104 = 20.1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the discrete probabilistic task.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, success clamp variability decreased with age (R2=0.048, F1,104 = 5.25, p=0.024).
source: In addition, success clamp variability decreased with age (R2=0.048, F1,104 = 5.25, p=0.024).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the discrete probabilistic task.

claim: The variability after failure had a higher intercept (increase of 41%; p=0.048) for the discrete probabilistic group compared to continuous probabilistic group.
source: However, the variability after failure had a higher intercept (increase of 41%; p=0.048) for the discrete probabilistic group, consistent with increasing exploration in the younger children.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison between groups.

claim: The intercept for distance to target was lower (decrease of 41%; p=0.007) for the discrete probabilistic group compared to continuous probabilistic group.
source: In addition, the intercept was lower for the distance to target (decrease of 41%; p=0.007), consistent with better learning in the younger children with discrete targets.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical comparison between groups.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, exploration increased significantly with age (p<0.001).
source: Exploration increased significantly with age (p<0.001; Figure 6b), but the motor noise change with age was not significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: In the discrete probabilistic task, motor noise change with age was not significant.
source: Exploration increased significantly with age (p<0.001; Figure 6b), but the motor noise change with age was not significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean age between the four tasks (F3,168=1.072, p=0.362).
source: There was no significant difference in mean age between the four tasks (F3,168=1.072, p=0.362) nor was there a significant interaction between task and sex on learning (F3,164=0.97, p=0.409).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results comparing age across tasks.

claim: There was no significant interaction between task and sex on learning (F3,164=0.97, p=0.409).
source: There was no significant difference in mean age between the four tasks (F3,168=1.072, p=0.362) nor was there a significant interaction between task and sex on learning (F3,164=0.97, p=0.409).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: An ANOVA of final learning showed a significant effect of Target type (discrete better than continuous; F1,168=12.87, p<0.001).
source: An ANOVA of final learning (Figure 7 left panel) showed a significant effect of Target type (discrete better than continuous; F1,168=12.87, p<0.001) and Reward landscape (deterministic better than probabilistic; F1,168=43.66, p<0.001) with no interaction (F1,168=0.24, p=0.628).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 7.

claim: An ANOVA of final learning showed a significant effect of Reward landscape (deterministic better than probabilistic; F1,168=43.66, p<0.001).
source: An ANOVA of final learning (Figure 7 left panel) showed a significant effect of Target type (discrete better than continuous; F1,168=12.87, p<0.001) and Reward landscape (deterministic better than probabilistic; F1,168=43.66, p<0.001) with no interaction (F1,168=0.24, p=0.628).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 7.

claim: There was no interaction between Target type and Reward landscape on final learning (F1,168=0.24, p=0.628).
source: An ANOVA of final learning (Figure 7 left panel) showed a significant effect of Target type (discrete better than continuous; F1,168=12.87, p<0.001) and Reward landscape (deterministic better than probabilistic; F1,168=43.66, p<0.001) with no interaction (F1,168=0.24, p=0.628).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Learning was worst under the continuous probabilistic task for 3-8 year olds.
source: Learning was worst under the continuous probabilistic task, followed by the discrete probabilistic task and continuous deterministic task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about relative learning performance across tasks.

claim: The 3–8 year olds performed best on the discrete deterministic task.
source: The 3–8 year olds performed best on the discrete deterministic task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about learning performance in the discrete deterministic task.

claim: Making the task discrete or deterministic improves learning and these factors were additive.
source: This shows that making the task discrete or deterministic improves learning and that these factors were additive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ANOVA results showing main effects without interaction.

claim: Improvement in learning was not due to significant differences in baseline precision across the four tasks.
source: This improvement in learning was not due to significant differences in baseline precision (Figure 7b 2nd panel; ANOVA gave Target type: F1,168 = 0.16, p=0.69, Reward landscape: F1,168 = 0.56, p=0.455, interaction: F1,168 = 1.71, p=0.192).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 7b.

claim: For the success clamp block, there was no main effect of Target type (F1,168=0.07, p=0.79).
source: For the success clamp block, there was no main effect of Target type (F1,168=0.07, p=0.79), but a main effect of Reward landscape (F1,168=6.71, p=0.01; less variability with a deterministic landscape) with no interaction (F1,168=3.58, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the success clamp.

claim: For the success clamp block, there was a main effect of Reward landscape (F1,168=6.71, p=0.01; less variability with a deterministic landscape).
source: For the success clamp block, there was no main effect of Target type (F1,168=0.07, p=0.79), but a main effect of Reward landscape (F1,168=6.71, p=0.01; less variability with a deterministic landscape) with no interaction (F1,168=3.58, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the success clamp.

claim: For the fail clamp block, there was a main effect of both Target type (F1,168=29.93, p<0.001; greater variability for discrete targets) and Reward landscape (F1,168=9.26, p=0.003; greater variability with a deterministic landscape).
source: For the fail clamp block, there was a main effect of both Target type (F1,168=29.93, p<0.001; greater variability for discrete targets) and Reward landscape (F1,168=9.26, p=0.003; greater variability with a deterministic landscape) with no interaction (F1,168=1.01, p=0.316).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results for the fail clamp.

claim: The increased variability for discrete targets in the fail clamp is likely because participants must move to a new target to explore, resulting in a larger position change.
source: The increased variability for discrete targets is likely because participants must move to a new target to explore, resulting in a larger position change.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed effect.

claim: Increased variability after failure in the deterministic landscape is likely because a failure at one location predicts there will never be success at that location.
source: Increased variability after failure in the deterministic landscape is likely because a failure at one location predicts there will never be success at that location (in contrast to the probabilistic tasks), thereby encouraging exploration.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed effect.

claim: Even young children choose their exploration in a rational way based on task features.
source: These show that even young children choose their exploration in a rational way based on task features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of exploration variability across different task conditions.

claim: Motor noise was significantly affected by Reward landscape (F1,168=35.5, p<0.001) but not by Target type.
source: Examination of the fit parameters for these groups (Figure 7c) showed that motor noise was significantly affected by Reward landscape (F1,168=35.5, p<0.001) but not by Target type.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 7c.

claim: Exploration variability was significantly affected by Reward landscape (F1,168=60.1, p<0.001) and Target type (F1,168=16.6, p<0.001).
source: Exploration variability was significantly affected by Reward landscape (F1,168=60.1, p<0.001) and Target type (F1,168=16.6, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: As motor noise increases, the optimal amount of exploration variability decreases.
source: These simulations showed that as motor noise increases, the optimal amount of exploration variability decreases (white lines; see Appendix 1 for a proof of this relation).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model simulations with reference to a proof in Appendix 1.

claim: In general, the children did not produce the optimal amount of exploration.
source: Although the same trend is seen in the model fits to the children's behavior (gray bars), in general, the children did not produce the optimal amount of exploration.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing observed behavior to optimal behavior predicted by the model.

claim: 16 participants completed the continuous probabilistic task in the lab, including five participants in the 3- to 8-year-old age range.
source: First, 16 participants completed the continuous probabilistic task in the lab, and this sample included five participants in the 3- to 8-year-old age range.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the in-lab sample composition.

claim: In-lab participants were able to accurately describe the goal of the task.
source: These in-lab participants were able to accurately describe the goal of the task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about task comprehension based on informal assessment.

claim: Performance for all participants tested in the lab was not significantly different from online completion.
source: Performance for all participants tested in the lab was not significantly different from online completion, and these data points are indicated in Figures 2 and 4 with white symbols.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison between in-lab and online performance.

claim: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed no significant difference between in-lab and online participants in baseline mean (Z = 1.238, p=0.216).
source: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed no significant difference between in-lab and online participants in baseline mean (Z = 1.238, p=0.216), baseline precision (Z = –0.626, p=0.532), distance from target (Z = –0.348, p=0.728), success clamp variability (Z = –1.952, p=0.051), fail clamp variability (Z = 0.281, p=0.779), or single target mean (Z = –0.399, p=0.690).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results comparing in-lab and online performance.

claim: In the 3- to 5-year-old group for the discrete deterministic condition, 18 out of 21 had performance better fit by the preferred model.
source: In the 3- to 5-year-old group for the discrete deterministic condition, 18 out of 21 had performance better fit by the preferred model, suggesting this age group understands the basic task of moving in different directions to find a rewarding location.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model fit results for the youngest age group.

claim: The reduced numbers fit by the preferred model for other conditions likely reflect differences in the task conditions (continuous and/or probabilistic) rather than a lack of understanding of the goal of the task.
source: The reduced numbers fit by the preferred model for the other conditions likely reflect differences in the task conditions (continuous and/or probabilistic) rather than a lack of understanding of the goal of the task.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of model fit results.

claim: Older children (9-17 years) and adults learned more than younger children (3-8 years) in the continuous probabilistic task.
source: We found a developmental trajectory of reinforcement learning in the continuous probabilistic task, with older children learning more than younger children.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main finding of developmental differences in learning.

claim: The developmental trajectory of learning was paralleled by age-dependent increases in exploration after a failed trial.
source: This was paralleled by age-dependent increases in exploration after a failed trial, which is essential for learning and decreases in baseline movement precision.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the parallel developmental changes observed.

claim: Younger children (3-8 years) had the fundamental mechanisms for interpreting binary reward signals to drive reinforcement learning of movement.
source: Thus, the youngest children had the fundamental mechanisms for interpreting binary reward signals to drive reinforcement learning of movement—this is not surprising given that this ability has been shown in infants (Rovee and Rovee, 1969).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the performance in the discrete deterministic task, supported by citation to infant research.

claim: Children aged 3–8 did not effectively utilize reward signals to learn in situations where they had to respond to probabilistic environments or where there were no spatial cues specifying distinct targets.
source: However, children aged 3–8 did not effectively utilize reward signals to learn in situations where they had to respond to probabilistic environments or where there were no spatial cues specifying distinct targets.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the limitations observed in young children's learning.

claim: The developmental trajectory identified was not due to poor motor accuracy in younger children.
source: Our data suggest that the developmental trajectory we identified was not due to poor motor accuracy or lack of understanding of the task in the younger children.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the baseline performance data showing accurate target hitting.

claim: The developmental trajectory identified was not due to lack of understanding of the task in younger children.
source: Our data suggest that the developmental trajectory we identified was not due to poor motor accuracy or lack of understanding of the task in the younger children.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from task comprehension assessments and model fit analyses.

claim: The youngest children could learn similarly to adults in the discrete deterministic task.
source: The youngest children could also learn similarly to adults in the discrete deterministic task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about performance in the discrete deterministic task.

claim: The preferred model was a special case (with no exploration after success) of the model proposed in Therrien et al., 2018.
source: We found that the preferred model was a special case (with no exploration after success) of the model proposed in Therrien et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between the preferred model and previous models in the literature.

claim: Variability in the task is due to motor noise as well as active exploration after failure.
source: This suggests that variability in our task is due to motor noise as well as active exploration after failure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preferred model structure.

claim: The desired reach is updated by the exploration present on a successful trial which was preceded by a failure trial.
source: The desired reach is updated by the exploration present on a successful trial which was preceded by a failure trial (the necessary condition for exploration).
evidence: This is a direct description of the update rule in the preferred model.

claim: Exploration can decrease with age in some studies, indicating that adults explore less compared to children.
source: Some other studies of development have shown that exploration can decrease with age, indicating that adults explore less compared to children (Schulz et al., 2019; Meder et al., 2021; Giron et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing different developmental patterns.

claim: The divergence between this study and previous findings is largely due to the experimental design and the role of motor noise.
source: We believe the divergence between our work and these previous findings is largely due to the experimental design of our study and the role of motor noise.
evidence: This is an inference about why the current findings differ from previous research.

claim: As motor noise goes down through development, the optimal amount of exploration goes up.
source: As we show in simulations of our task, as motor noise goes down (as it is known to do through development), the optimal amount of exploration goes up (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model simulations with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Appendix 1.

claim: The behavior of participants is rational in terms of increasing exploration as motor noise decreases.
source: Therefore, the behavior of our participants is rational in terms of increasing exploration as motor noise decreases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing observed behavior to optimal behavior predicted by the model.

claim: Older children make larger adjustments after failure compared to younger children to find the highly rewarded zone more quickly.
source: Older children make larger adjustments after failure compared to younger children to find the highly rewarded zone more quickly.
evidence: This is a direct statement about age-related differences in exploration behavior.

claim: 6- to 12-year-old children increased throwing variability after missed trials and minimized variability after successful trials in a real-world throwing task.
source: Konrad et al., 2025 have recently shown this behavior in a real-world throwing task where 6- to 12-year-old children increased throwing variability after missed trials and minimized variability after successful trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research (Konrad et al., 2025).

claim: Participants were more variable after non-rewarded trials compared to rewarded trials in a postural motor control task.
source: This has also been shown in a postural motor control task where participants were more variable after non-rewarded trials compared to rewarded trials (van Mastrigt et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (van Mastrigt et al., 2020).

claim: The optimal amount of exploration is dependent on the specifics of the task.
source: In general, these studies suggest that the optimal amount of exploration is dependent on the specifics of the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings across multiple studies.

claim: The continuous target task relies more on spatial working memory, which is not fully developed.
source: We suspect that the continuous target task relies more on spatial working memory, which is not fully developed (van Asselen et al., 2006), particularly in those under 10 years of age (Hitch et al., 1988; Pickering, 2001; Tsujii et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about the cognitive demands of the task, supported by citations to developmental research on spatial working memory.

claim: Younger children may benefit from clear markers in the environment to differentiate various spatial positions along the target.
source: Younger children may benefit from clear markers in the environment to differentiate various spatial positions along the target.
evidence: This is a speculation about why discrete targets improved learning in younger children.

claim: Children find it easier to select from discrete choices on a Likert scale versus using a continuous visual analog scale.
source: This is consistent with tasks that have assessed children's preferences for reporting information; they find it easier to select from discrete choices on a Likert scale versus using a continuous visual analog scale (van Laerhoven et al., 2004; Shields et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on children's response preferences.

claim: Phonological encoding using verbal labels develops later than visual encoding and both can be used to hold information in working memory.
source: It is known that phonological encoding using verbal labels develops later than visual encoding and both can be used to hold information in working memory (e.g. my last movement was near the left edge of the screen) (Pickering, 2001; Hitch et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on working memory development.

claim: The deterministic landscape is less ambiguous than the probabilistic landscape because participants always fail if they are outside the 100% reward zone.
source: The deterministic landscape is less ambiguous than the probabilistic landscape by design—participants always fail if they are outside the 100% reward zone.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design difference between deterministic and probabilistic reward landscapes.

claim: Younger children take longer to choose a reward maximization strategy in a probabilistic environment where all choices have the possibility of being rewarded.
source: Younger children have been reported to take longer to choose a reward maximization strategy in a probabilistic environment where all choices have the possibility of being rewarded.
evidence: This is a general statement about previous research findings on children's decision-making strategies.

claim: When children and adults choose between eight options, they initially probability match, but adults switch over to a maximizing strategy more quickly than children.
source: Plate et al., 2018 showed that when children and adults choose between eight options, they initially probability match (i.e. the frequency of selection closely matches the frequency of reward on the various task options). However, adults switch over to a maximizing strategy (i.e. choosing the highest reward option) more quickly than children (Plate et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Plate et al., 2018).

claim: In a deterministic landscape, probability matching would result in the same behavior as reward maximizing.
source: In a deterministic landscape, probability matching would result in the same behavior as reward maximizing and therefore the younger children's behavior would appear nearly the same as adults.
evidence: This is an inference about why younger children performed better in the deterministic task.

claim: Young children's behavior may stem from a fundamental need to prioritize hypothesis testing and gathering information about the world.
source: Young children's behavior may also stem from a fundamental need to prioritize hypothesis testing and gathering information about the world (Schulz et al., 2019; Liquin and Gopnik, 2022; Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019), a discovery process that facilitates increased knowledge about the environment's causal structure (Sobel and Sommerville, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the cognitive motivations underlying young children's exploration behavior, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Poorer learning performance in tasks besides discrete deterministic was due to an inability to effectively utilize probabilistic reward signals or find the high reward location without clearly delineated spatial cues.
source: Our interpretation is that poorer learning performance in tasks besides discrete deterministic was due to an inability to effectively utilize probabilistic reward signals or find the high reward location without clearly delineated spatial cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of results across the four tasks.

claim: Most objects in the world do not have delineated targets on them; we learn which location on an object leads to reward by exploring different options.
source: This has significant ramifications as most objects in the world do not have delineated targets on them; we learn which location on an object leads to reward by exploring different options (e.g. the best location to grab a mug or push a heavy door open).
evidence: This is a general statement about real-world learning situations based on common knowledge.

claim: The world is not deterministic, as it is rare that the same action will always give the same result.
source: The world is also not deterministic, as it is rare that the same action will always give the same result.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of real-world environments based on common knowledge.

claim: Movement outcomes are probabilistic due to both environmental variation and motor noise.
source: Movement outcomes are probabilistic due to both environmental variation and motor noise (e.g. the direction of a soccer ball when kicked on different fields or the location of a thrown dart on a dartboard).
evidence: This is a general statement about sources of variability in movement outcomes based on common knowledge.

claim: The differential ability to incorporate reward signals into changes in behavior across childhood may stem from maturation of the reward centers in the brain.
source: The differential ability to incorporate reward signals into changes in behavior across childhood may stem from maturation of the reward centers in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural basis of the developmental changes observed.

claim: Structures important for reinforcement learning, such as the basal ganglia reward centers, dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and the anterior cingulate cortex develop throughout childhood.
source: Structures important for these processes, such as the basal ganglia reward centers, dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and the anterior cingulate cortex develop throughout childhood (Raznahan et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2000; Schultz, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain development.

claim: The pallidum reaches peak volume at 9.5 years for females and 7.7 years for males.
source: As a main underlying neural structure of reinforcement learning, the pallidum reaches peak volume at 9.5 years for females and 7.7 years for males while it takes the thalamus until 13.8 years for females and 17.4 years for males to reach peak volume (Raznahan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Raznahan et al., 2014).

claim: The thalamus reaches peak volume at 13.8 years for females and 17.4 years for males.
source: As a main underlying neural structure of reinforcement learning, the pallidum reaches peak volume at 9.5 years for females and 7.7 years for males while it takes the thalamus until 13.8 years for females and 17.4 years for males to reach peak volume (Raznahan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Raznahan et al., 2014).

claim: Older children have more mature brain circuits and may be better able to take advantage of strategies in probabilistic environments that younger children cannot.
source: Older children have more mature brain circuits and may be better able to take advantage of strategies in probabilistic environments that younger children cannot (Schulz et al., 2019; Liquin and Gopnik, 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation about the relationship between brain maturation and learning strategies, supported by citations.

claim: Brain activity in younger children can be similar after positive and negative rewards, whereas in older children and adults, it is more distinct.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that brain activity in younger children can be similar after positive and negative rewards, whereas in older children and adults, it is more distinct (Mai et al., 2011; Eppinger et al., 2009; van Meel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: The study was conducted remotely without control of computer operating quality, internet speed, or testing environment.
source: Given that this task was conducted remotely, we did not have control of the computer operating quality, internet speed, or testing environment for our participants (see Methods for exclusion criteria).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of the remote study design.

claim: The study was not able to control or analyze timing parameters of movement in detail.
source: As such, we were not able to control or analyze timing parameters of movement in detail, which can be done more easily in in-person experimentation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a limitation of the remote study design.

claim: The key analyses compare across large groups that likely factor out uncontrolled variables.
source: However, our key analyses compare across large groups that likely factor out these uncontrolled variables.
evidence: This is a statement about how the study design addresses potential confounds.

claim: Other processes, such as memory and motivation, could affect performance on these tasks.
source: We also recognize that other processes, such as memory and motivation, could affect performance on these tasks; however, our study was not designed to test these processes directly, and future work would benefit from exploring these other components more explicitly.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential confounding factors and a suggestion for future research.

claim: The findings in typical development lay a foundation for better understanding of behavior during childhood and could help inform what function may be lost or impaired after injury.
source: Our findings in typical development lay a foundation for better understanding of behavior during childhood and could help inform what function may be lost or impaired after injury.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential implications of the research findings.

claim: There is a need to consider not only disease process for interventions but also age, as there are developmental differences in motor learning capacity in individuals at different ages.
source: This underscores the need to consider not only disease process for interventions but also age, as there are developmental differences in motor learning capacity in individuals at different ages.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical implications of the research findings.

claim: Knowing how the sensorimotor system works at different ages can guide decisions on how to intervene or alter an environment and give children the best opportunity to use reinforcement learning mechanisms for rehabilitation outcomes.
source: Knowing how the sensorimotor system works at different ages can guide decisions on how to intervene or alter an environment and give children the best opportunity to use reinforcement learning mechanisms for rehabilitation outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the research findings to rehabilitation.

claim: A total of 385 complete datasets were included in the analysis.
source: A total of 385 complete datasets were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size.

claim: Participants were recruited from 38 states out of the 50 United States of America.
source: Our sample includes participants from 38 states out of the 50 United States of America (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the geographic distribution of the sample with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study was approved by the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Institutional Review Board.
source: This study was approved by the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Institutional Review Board and all participants, or their parent/legal guardian, provided informed consent prior to participation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants, or their parent/legal guardian, provided informed consent prior to participation.
source: This study was approved by the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Institutional Review Board and all participants, or their parent/legal guardian, provided informed consent prior to participation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the consent process.

claim: Movement trajectories were sampled at the polling rate of the selected input device.
source: Movement trajectories were sampled at the polling rate of the selected input device, and data from each trial were uploaded and saved to Google Firebase Realtime Database at the end of each trial.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection method.

claim: Data sampling rates of input devices had a mean of 37.363 ±4.184 Hz.
source: Each trial was manually inspected and sampling rates of input devices had a mean of 37.363 ±4.184 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sampling rate characteristics.
